# How to use this guide

Adult Health Nursing II (N-AHN(II)225) is the continuation of Adult Health Nursing I, moving from the foundational medical-surgical nursing you studied in Semester 3 into specialist systems — ENT, eyes, kidneys and urinary tract, burns and reconstructive surgery, neurology, HIV/AIDS and oncology, emergency and critical care, and geriatric and occupational health nursing. It is a large and demanding subject and accounts for a significant portion of the Semester 4 theory examination marks. Study it in parallel with Pathology II and Pharmacology II, because those subjects explain the diseases and drugs you will use in your AHN-II patient care.

## Exam pattern

N-AHN(II)225 is examined at the end of Semester 4 as a **standalone theory paper** following the standard INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing exam format. Confirm the exact paper pattern and marking scheme with your college, as universities may print the paper in slightly different formats.

**Typical INC B.Sc Nursing end-semester theory paper (75 marks, 3 hours)**

| Section | Type | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 20 objective questions (MCQ or fill-in-the-blank) — attempt all | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 questions | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 questions | 7 × 5 = 35 |
| **Total** | | **75** |

There is no internal choice in Section A. Section B and C give you a choice of which questions to attempt. Always read all Section C questions before choosing — pick the ones you can answer most fully.

## How the unit files are arranged

The INC 2021 syllabus for N-AHN(II)225 has eight numbered units. This pack keeps **one notes file per INC unit**, so the numbers match directly.

| Notes file | INC unit | Topics covered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 — ENT nursing | I | Ear (hearing loss, otitis, mastoidectomy), nose (sinusitis, epistaxis, septoplasty), throat (tonsillitis, laryngitis, tracheostomy) |
| Unit 2 — Eye nursing | II | Refractive errors, conjunctivitis, cataract, glaucoma, retinal detachment, blindness, eye donation |
| Unit 3 — Kidney and urinary | III | Assessment, UTI, incontinence, retention, calculi, GN, nephrotic syndrome, AKI, CKD, dialysis, BPH, prostate cancer |
| Unit 4 — Burns and reconstruction | IV | Burn classification, Rule of Nines, Parkland formula, wound care, grafting, contracture prevention, reconstruction, cosmetic surgery |
| Unit 5 — Neurological nursing | V | GCS, raised ICP, headache, epilepsy, status epilepticus, stroke, meningitis, Parkinson's, spinal cord injury, unconscious patient care |
| Unit 6 — HIV/AIDS and oncology | VI | Immune system, HIV staging and ART, opportunistic infections, chemo administration, radiotherapy, cancer pain, palliative care |
| Unit 7 — Emergency and critical care | VII | Triage, BCLS, anaphylaxis, MI, stroke, DKA, poisoning, ventilator care bundle, disaster nursing |
| Unit 8 — Geriatric and occupational | VIII | Ageing changes, geriatric assessment, dementia/delirium, falls, elder abuse, occupational diseases, ergonomics |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Start every answer with the nursing assessment.** For any disorder, the examiner expects you to describe how you would recognise and assess the patient before discussing management. Use the nursing process frame: Assessment → Nursing Diagnosis → Planning → Intervention → Evaluation.

2. **Learn the BCLS sequence precisely.** The sequence (C–A–B, 30:2, rate 100–120, depth 5–6 cm, AED steps) is asked every year — in Section A as single MCQs and in Section C as a short answer.

3. **Distinguish airway management priorities.** In emergencies — anaphylaxis, status epilepticus, unconscious patient — airway comes first. Name the specific airway technique used (recovery position, oropharyngeal airway, endotracheal intubation, tracheostomy).

4. **Give pathophysiology before management.** Even in a 5-mark short answer, one sentence of pathophysiology (why the problem occurs) lifts the answer above a nursing-care list.

5. **Use comparison tables.** The examiner values a well-drawn table for: burn degrees (look vs sensation vs healing), nephritic vs nephrotic syndrome, AKI vs CKD, delirium vs dementia, ischaemic vs haemorrhagic stroke. Practise drawing each from memory.

6. **Name drugs with their class.** For ART, name at least one drug per class (NRTI, NNRTI, PI, INSTI). For cancer pain, state the WHO ladder step and an example drug at each step. For epilepsy, name the AED and its main side effect.

7. **For long essays (10 marks):** use a structured heading for each of the five standard areas (definition/classification, causes/risk factors, clinical features, investigations, management and nursing care) and write 2–3 lines per heading. This reliably scores 7–8 marks even if your knowledge of one area is limited.

8. **End every nursing-care answer with patient education.** At least one or two discharge teaching points show the examiner that you think of the whole patient, not just the hospital stay.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most years; commit the full answer to memory.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a broader question.
- **Low** — appears rarely; useful for MCQs and to round off a long essay.

These ratings are estimates based on the weight of each topic in the INC syllabus and common patterns in B.Sc Nursing university papers. They are a guide, not a guarantee.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Notes file | High-probability topics |
| --- | --- |
| 1 ENT | Tracheostomy care, mastoidectomy post-op, epistaxis management |
| 2 Eye | Cataract and post-op care, glaucoma, eye donation, chemical eye injury first aid |
| 3 Kidney | AKI vs CKD (table), dialysis (haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis), nephritic vs nephrotic, renal diet, catheter care |
| 4 Burns | Parkland formula, Rule of Nines, burn wound care, contracture prevention |
| 5 Neurology | GCS, Cushing's triad, epilepsy seizure management and status epilepticus, stroke (ischaemic vs haemorrhagic), unconscious patient care |
| 6 HIV/AIDS | HIV staging, ART classes (name one drug each), opportunistic infections, nursing care including PEP and stigma |
| 7 Emergency | BCLS sequence, anaphylaxis (adrenaline IM dose), DKA management, poisoning antidotes |
| 8 Geriatric | Delirium vs dementia, fall prevention, occupational lung diseases (silicosis, asbestosis) |

# Last-night revision sheet

Print this, fold it in half, and carry it to the exam hall. These are the numbers, sequences and comparisons that appear as MCQs and short answers every year.

---

## Key numbers to memorise

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| BCLS compression rate | 100–120 per minute |
| BCLS compression depth | 5–6 cm |
| BCLS compression:breath ratio | 30:2 |
| Anaphylaxis — adrenaline dose | 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM, lateral thigh |
| DKA — first fluid (first hour) | 0.9% NaCl 1 L |
| DKA insulin infusion rate | 0.1 unit/kg/hour |
| GCS maximum score | 15 (E4 V5 M6) |
| GCS score indicating intubation needed | ≤ 8 |
| Cushing's triad | Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respirations |
| WHO CD4 threshold for AIDS | < 200 cells/µL |
| WHO CD4 threshold for PCP prophylaxis | < 200 cells/µL (cotrimoxazole) |
| Parkland formula | 4 mL × kg × %TBSA; half in 8 hours, half in next 16 hours |
| Rule of Nines — head and neck | 9% |
| Rule of Nines — each arm | 9% |
| Rule of Nines — chest / abdomen | 18% each (anterior trunk 36% total) |
| Rule of Nines — each leg | 18% |
| Rule of Nines — perineum | 1% |
| Braden Scale risk threshold | ≤ 18 |
| Morse Fall Scale risk threshold | ≥ 45 |
| MMSE: mild impairment | 18–23 |
| MMSE: severe impairment | < 10 |
| GDS (15-item): depression likely | ≥ 5 |
| Neutropenic sepsis — IV antibiotics target | Within 1 hour of fever |
| Neutrophil count for reverse barrier nursing | < 0.5 × 10⁹/L |
| Paracetamol overdose antidote | N-acetylcysteine; most effective within 8 hours |
| INC B.Sc Nursing exam total marks | 75 marks, 3 hours |

---

## Must-know comparisons

### AKI vs CKD

| Feature | AKI | CKD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Sudden (hours to days) | Gradual (months to years) |
| Kidney size on USS | Normal or enlarged | Small, shrunken |
| Creatinine | Rises rapidly | Gradually elevated |
| Anaemia | Less common early | Yes (erythropoietin deficiency) |
| Reversibility | Often reversible | Irreversible; progressive |
| Bone disease | Not initially | Renal osteodystrophy (↑PTH, ↓Ca, ↑PO₄) |

### Nephritic vs Nephrotic syndrome

| Feature | Nephritic | Nephrotic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proteinuria | Mild | Massive (> 3.5 g/day) |
| Haematuria | Yes (RBC casts in urine) | Minimal |
| Oedema | Mild (periorbital) | Generalised (anasarca) |
| Hypertension | Yes | Variable |
| Serum albumin | Normal/mildly low | Very low (< 25 g/L) |
| Example cause | Post-strep GN, IgA nephropathy | Minimal change disease (children), membranous GN |

### Ischaemic vs Haemorrhagic stroke

| Feature | Ischaemic | Haemorrhagic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Clot blocks artery | Blood vessel ruptures |
| Onset | May be gradual / TIA precursor | Sudden, often with headache |
| CT head | Hypodense (dark) area | Hyperdense (white) blood |
| Thrombolysis (tPA) | Yes — if within 4.5 h, no contraindication | CONTRAINDICATED |
| Preceding headache | Unusual | Common (worst headache of life — SAH) |

### Delirium vs Dementia

| Feature | Delirium | Dementia |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Acute (hours to days) | Gradual (months to years) |
| Course | Fluctuating during the day | Progressive, stable day to day |
| Consciousness | Impaired (clouded) | Clear until late stages |
| Attention | Severely impaired | Less affected early |
| Reversibility | Often reversible | Irreversible (most types) |
| Main causes | Infection, drugs, constipation, metabolic | Alzheimer's, vascular, Lewy body |

### Burns — depth classification

| Degree | Old name | Appearance | Sensation | Healing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Superficial | First degree | Red, dry, no blisters | Painful | 3–5 days; no scar |
| Superficial partial thickness | Second degree | Red, blistered, moist | Very painful | 7–21 days; minimal scar |
| Deep partial thickness | Deep second degree | Pale/mottled, moist or leathery | Reduced pain | > 21 days; often needs grafting |
| Full thickness | Third degree | White/grey/black, dry, leathery | No pain (nerve destroyed) | Cannot heal; requires grafting |

---

## Sequences to draw from memory

### BCLS sequence (adult)

```text
   Safe? → Check responsiveness → Call for help + get AED
   → Check breathing (≤ 10 s, no normal breathing = arrest)
   → Compressions: heel of hand, lower sternum
     Rate: 100–120/min | Depth: 5–6 cm | Full recoil | 30:2
   → Open airway (head-tilt chin-lift)
   → 2 rescue breaths (each 1 s, watch chest rise)
   → Repeat 30:2 until AED arrives or signs of life
   → AED: on → pads → analyse → no contact → shock → CPR 2 min → re-analyse
```

### Anaphylaxis management

```text
   1. Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM lateral thigh — FIRST
   2. Call for emergency help
   3. Position: supine + legs raised (if no respiratory distress)
   4. 100% O₂ via non-rebreather mask
   5. IV access + 0.9% NaCl 500–1000 mL bolus
   6. Chlorpheniramine 10 mg IV (secondary — for skin)
   7. Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV (secondary — late phase)
   8. Salbutamol nebulised (for bronchospasm)
   9. Repeat adrenaline every 5–15 min if no improvement
   10. Admit; observe 6–12 hours (biphasic reaction risk)
```

### DKA management

```text
   Fluids: 0.9% NaCl 1 L/h → 1 L/2h → 1 L/4h
   Insulin: 0.1 unit/kg/h IV (start after first litre of fluid)
   K⁺: add to fluids once K⁺ < 5.5 mmol/L + urine output
   Monitor: glucose hourly, electrolytes 2-hourly, urine output
   Switch: IV→SC insulin when eating + glucose < 14 mmol/L
   Add 10% dextrose when glucose < 14 to protect brain
```

### Status epilepticus sequence

```text
   0–5 min:  Protect airway, recovery position, O₂, IV access, glucose
   5–10 min: Lorazepam 4 mg IV (or diazepam 10 mg IV/PR)
   10–20 min: Repeat benzodiazepine if still seizing
   20–30 min: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV infusion (or levetiracetam)
   > 30 min:  Anaesthetic agent (propofol/thiopentone) + ICU intubation
```

### Glasgow Coma Scale — quick recall

```text
   Eye opening:   4 Spontaneous | 3 To voice | 2 To pain | 1 None
   Verbal:        5 Oriented | 4 Confused | 3 Words | 2 Sounds | 1 None
   Motor:         6 Obeys | 5 Localises | 4 Withdraws | 3 Flexion | 2 Extension | 1 None
   Maximum = 15 | Intubate if ≤ 8 | Minimum = 3
```

---

## Normal laboratory values (nursing-relevant)

| Test | Normal adult range |
| --- | --- |
| Serum sodium (Na⁺) | 135–145 mmol/L |
| Serum potassium (K⁺) | 3.5–5.0 mmol/L |
| Serum creatinine | 60–110 µmol/L (female lower) |
| Blood urea | 2.5–7.1 mmol/L |
| Fasting blood glucose | 3.9–5.5 mmol/L |
| pH (arterial) | 7.35–7.45 |
| SpO₂ (normal) | 95–100% |
| Haemoglobin: male | 130–180 g/L |
| Haemoglobin: female | 120–160 g/L |
| Neutrophil count | 2.0–7.5 × 10⁹/L |
| Platelet count | 150–400 × 10⁹/L |
| CD4 count (healthy) | 500–1500 cells/µL |
| Serum albumin | 35–50 g/L |

---

## ART drug classes — one drug each (exam minimum)

| Class | Remember one drug |
| --- | --- |
| NRTI | Tenofovir (TDF) |
| NNRTI | Efavirenz |
| PI | Lopinavir/ritonavir |
| INSTI | Dolutegravir (DTG) |
| India first-line | TDF + 3TC + DTG (once daily) |

---

## WHO analgesic ladder (3 steps)

```text
   Step 1 (mild pain):    Paracetamol ± NSAID ± adjuvant
   Step 2 (moderate):     Weak opioid (codeine / tramadol) ± Step 1
   Step 3 (severe):       Strong opioid (morphine / fentanyl) ± Step 1
   Always: by mouth | by the clock | by the ladder | laxative with every opioid
```

---

## Occupational lung diseases — one-line each

| Disease | Cause | Key fact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Silicosis | Crystalline silica (mining, quarrying) | Upper lobe fibrosis; ↑TB risk |
| Asbestosis | Asbestos fibres (construction, shipbuilding) | 20–40 year latency; mesothelioma risk |
| Coal workers' pneumoconiosis | Coal dust | Simple → progressive massive fibrosis |
| NIHL | > 85 dB noise | Starts at 4 kHz; irreversible |

---

## Exam reminder

- Section A (20 marks): read carefully; eliminate wrong options first; never leave blank.
- Section B (20 marks): write 2 of 3 essays; use the 5-part structure (definition/classification → causes → features → investigations → management + nursing care); 10 marks = 5 × 2-mark points well written.
- Section C (35 marks): 7 of 9 short answers; choose the ones you know best; 2 marks go to any answer that shows you understand the question — always write something.
- For any emergency/procedure answer: state the nursing priorities in order (what comes first, second, third) and name specific drugs with dose and route.
- For any comparison question: draw a two-column table — it shows the examiner you can synthesise, and it is faster to write than prose.
- If you run out of time: outline-and-leave — a heading with 3–4 bullet points scores more than a blank page.

# Unit 1 — Nursing management of disorders of the ear, nose and throat

This unit covers INC Unit I. It deals with the common medical and surgical problems of the ear, nose and throat (ENT), their causes, how they show, how they are diagnosed, and how the nurse cares for the patient. For each disorder, learn the pattern: cause (etiology) → what goes wrong (pathophysiology) → signs and symptoms → tests → medical/surgical treatment → nursing care and health education.

## 1.1 Review of anatomy and physiology

**Ear.** Three parts. The **external ear** (pinna and the external auditory canal up to the eardrum) collects and guides sound; the canal makes protective wax (cerumen). The **middle ear** is an air-filled cavity holding three tiny bones (malleus, incus, stapes) that carry vibration from the eardrum to the inner ear; the **Eustachian (auditory) tube** links it to the throat and equalises pressure. The **inner ear** has the **cochlea** (hearing) and the **vestibular system** (semicircular canals and vestibule, for balance). The eighth cranial nerve carries hearing and balance signals to the brain.

**Nose.** Warms, moistens and filters air, and holds the sense of smell. It has a rich blood supply; the front part of the septum (Little's area / Kiesselbach's plexus) bleeds easily. The paranasal sinuses (maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid) are air spaces that drain into the nose.

**Throat.** The pharynx is the shared passage for air and food; the larynx (voice box) holds the vocal cords and protects the airway during swallowing; the tonsils are lymphoid tissue guarding the throat.

## 1.2 Health history, physical assessment and diagnostic tests

Ask about pain (otalgia), discharge, hearing loss, ringing (tinnitus), giddiness (vertigo), nasal block, discharge, bleeding, loss of smell, sore throat, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. Note ear or chemical exposure, loud-noise work, and medicines that can harm the ear.

Physical examination uses **otoscopy** (looking at the canal and eardrum), the **tuning-fork tests** (Rinne and Weber, to tell conductive from sensorineural loss), **pure-tone audiometry** (a graph of the softest sounds heard at each pitch), **tympanometry** (middle-ear pressure and eardrum movement), **anterior and posterior rhinoscopy**, **nasal endoscopy**, X-ray/CT of the sinuses, indirect/direct **laryngoscopy**, and throat swab for culture.

```text
   EAR (simple cross-section)
   Pinna )  canal  | eardrum | malleus-incus-stapes | cochlea
   external ear    |        middle ear               | inner ear
                            Eustachian tube to throat
```

## 1.3 Disorders of the ear

**External ear.** *Deformities* may be present from birth (microtia). *Otalgia* (earache) may come from the ear itself or be referred from teeth, throat or jaw joint. *Foreign bodies* (insects, beads) are removed by syringing or forceps by trained staff; never push an object deeper. *Impacted wax* blocks the canal and dulls hearing; it is softened with drops and then syringed out with warm water. *Otitis externa* is infection of the canal (swimmer's ear) causing pain, itching and discharge, treated with cleaning and medicated drops.

**Middle ear.** *Tympanic membrane perforation* follows infection or injury and causes hearing loss and discharge; small holes often heal on their own, large ones may need surgical repair (myringoplasty/tympanoplasty). *Otitis media* is middle-ear infection:
- *Acute otitis media* — sudden pain, fever, reduced hearing, a bulging red eardrum; common in children because their Eustachian tube is short and flat. If pus builds up the drum may rupture and discharge.
- *Serous (secretous) otitis media* — fluid without acute infection, giving a blocked, muffled feeling.
- *Chronic suppurative otitis media* — long-standing discharge and perforation; may damage the ossicles and needs ear care, drops and sometimes surgery.
A **myringotomy** (a small cut in the eardrum, sometimes with a grommet tube) drains fluid.

**Inner ear.** *Ménière's disease* is excess fluid (endolymph) in the inner ear causing attacks of spinning vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and a feeling of fullness; a low-salt diet and medicines reduce attacks. *Labyrinthitis* is inflammation of the balance organ causing severe vertigo, nausea and unsteadiness. *Ototoxicity* is damage to the inner ear or its nerve by certain drugs (some antibiotics, diuretics, anti-cancer and anti-malarial drugs), shown by new hearing loss, tinnitus or imbalance; the nurse reports these early so the drug can be reviewed.

## 1.4 Disorders of the nose and throat

**Upper respiratory airway infections.** *Rhinitis* (runny, blocked, sneezing nose) may be infective or allergic. *Sinusitis* is infection of the sinuses with facial pain/pressure, blocked nose, thick discharge and fever; steam inhalation, decongestants and antibiotics help, and chronic cases may need endoscopic sinus surgery. *Tonsillitis* is sore red swollen tonsils with pain on swallowing and fever; repeated attacks may lead to **tonsillectomy**. *Laryngitis* is inflammation of the larynx causing hoarse voice and cough, helped by voice rest, fluids and steam.

**Epistaxis (nosebleed).** Caused by nose-picking, dry air, trauma, high blood pressure, infection or bleeding disorders. First aid: sit the patient up and lean forward (so blood does not run back and is not swallowed), pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for about 10 minutes, breathe through the mouth, and apply a cold pack to the bridge. If bleeding continues, the doctor may cauterise the vessel or insert an **anterior or posterior nasal pack**.

**Nasal obstruction** may come from a deviated septum, polyps, enlarged turbinates or growths; it is treated according to the cause, sometimes surgically.

**Laryngeal obstruction** is an emergency: swelling, a foreign body or a growth blocks the airway, giving noisy breathing (stridor), struggling to breathe and bluish colour (cyanosis). Clear the airway, give oxygen, and prepare for intubation or an emergency **tracheostomy**.

## 1.5 Deafness and its management

**Conductive deafness** is a block in the outer or middle ear (wax, fluid, perforation, ossicle problem); much of it can be corrected. **Sensorineural deafness** is damage to the cochlea or nerve (ageing, noise, drugs, infection); it is usually permanent and managed with hearing aids. **Mixed deafness** has both. Management includes removing the cause, hearing aids (devices that amplify sound), cochlear implants for severe nerve deafness, lip-reading and sign language, and prevention — ear protection against loud noise, careful use of ototoxic drugs, and early treatment of ear infections.

## 1.6 Nursing procedures and care (with rationale)

**Instilling ear drops.**
1. Check the order, warm the drops to body temperature in the hand — *cold drops cause giddiness.*
2. Position the patient lying with the affected ear up.
3. In an adult, pull the pinna up and back to straighten the canal; in a small child pull it down and back.
4. Drop the medicine along the side of the canal, not straight onto the drum.
5. Keep the position for a few minutes and gently press the tragus so the drops spread.

**Instilling nasal drops.** Position with the head tilted back (or lying with the head over the edge of the bed) so the medicine reaches the right area; ask the patient to breathe through the mouth and stay still for a few minutes.

**Nasal packing care.** Keep the patient sitting up, watch for bleeding at the back of the throat (swallowed blood), provide mouth care because the patient breathes through the mouth, and report headache or fresh bleeding.

**Tracheostomy care.** A tracheostomy is an opening in the windpipe with a tube.
1. Explain the procedure and reassure the patient, who cannot speak with the tube.
2. Keep a spare tube, obturator and dilator at the bedside — *so the airway can be re-opened if the tube comes out.*
3. Suction secretions using sterile technique, for no more than about ten seconds at a time, with oxygen before and after — *suction removes air as well as secretions.*
4. Clean the inner tube and the skin (stoma) around it, and change the dressing and tapes to prevent infection and skin damage.
5. Humidify the inspired air — *the nose that normally warms and moistens air is bypassed.*
6. Keep the patient in a semi-upright position, provide a call bell and a writing pad for communication.

**Hearing aid care.** Teach the patient to switch off and remove the aid at night, keep it dry, change or charge the battery, and clean the ear mould gently.

## Remember

- Ear = external (collects sound), middle (conducts sound, holds the three ossicles) and inner (cochlea for hearing, vestibular system for balance).
- Rinne and Weber tuning-fork tests separate conductive from sensorineural deafness; audiometry measures the hearing level.
- Acute otitis media is common in children because their Eustachian tube is short and flat; myringotomy drains the fluid.
- Ménière's disease = vertigo + fluctuating hearing loss + tinnitus + ear fullness; manage with a low-salt diet and medicines.
- Ototoxic drugs can cause new hearing loss, tinnitus or imbalance — report early.
- Epistaxis first aid: sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft nose for 10 minutes, breathe through the mouth, cold pack.
- Laryngeal obstruction and stridor are airway emergencies — oxygen and prepare for intubation or tracheostomy.
- For ear drops: adult pinna up and back, child down and back; warm the drops first.
- At every tracheostomy bedside keep a spare tube, obturator and dilator, suction and humidification.

# Unit 2 — Nursing management of disorders of the eye

This unit covers INC Unit II: common eye disorders, their causes, features, tests and management, and the nurse's role in eye donation, banking and transplantation. Learn each disorder as cause → change → signs → tests → treatment → nursing care and health teaching.

## 2.1 Review of anatomy and physiology

The eyeball has three coats. The outer coat is the tough white **sclera** at the back and the clear **cornea** in front (the cornea does most of the bending of light). The middle vascular coat is the **uvea** — the **iris** (coloured ring with the pupil in its centre), the **ciliary body** (makes aqueous fluid and changes the shape of the lens for focusing) and the **choroid**. The inner coat is the **retina**, which turns light into nerve signals carried by the optic nerve.

The clear **lens** sits behind the iris and fine-focuses light onto the retina. In front of the lens, the chamber is filled with watery **aqueous humour**, which is made and drained continuously; behind the lens the large cavity is filled with jelly-like **vitreous humour**. Tears from the lacrimal gland keep the front of the eye moist and drain through the puncta into the nose. Normal eye pressure (intraocular pressure) depends on a balance between aqueous made and aqueous drained.

```text
   EYE (side view, simplified)
   cornea -> aqueous -> iris/pupil -> lens -> vitreous -> retina -> optic nerve
   sclera forms the tough outer wall; choroid supplies blood; conjunctiva covers the front
```

## 2.2 History, physical and diagnostic assessment

Ask about blurred or reduced vision, pain, redness, watering, discharge, double vision, floaters, flashes of light, loss of part of the field of view, difficulty seeing at night, and any injury or chemical splash. Note diabetes and high blood pressure, which damage the retina.

Tests include **visual acuity** with a Snellen chart (distance vision) and near-vision charts; **refraction** to measure the spectacle number; **tonometry** to measure eye pressure; **ophthalmoscopy/fundoscopy** to view the retina and optic disc; **slit-lamp examination** of the front of the eye; perimetry for the field of vision; and colour-vision tests.

## 2.3 Refractive errors

The eye does not focus light exactly on the retina.
- **Myopia (short sight):** distant objects blur; the image falls in front of the retina; corrected with a concave (minus) lens.
- **Hypermetropia (long sight):** near objects blur; the image falls behind the retina; corrected with a convex (plus) lens.
- **Astigmatism:** uneven curve of the cornea blurs vision at all distances; corrected with a cylindrical lens.
- **Presbyopia:** age-related stiffening of the lens so near focus is lost, usually after the forties; corrected with reading glasses.
Refractive errors are also managed with contact lenses or corneal (laser) surgery.

## 2.4 Disorders of the eyelids and conjunctiva

- **Stye (hordeolum):** painful infected swelling at a lash root; warm compresses help it to point and drain.
- **Chalazion:** a painless firm lump from a blocked oil gland; may need a small incision.
- **Deformities:** *entropion* (lid turns in, lashes rub the eye) and *ectropion* (lid turns out, eye waters and dries); corrected by surgery.
- **Conjunctivitis:** inflammation of the conjunctiva — red eye, watering, discharge, gritty feeling. Infective (bacterial or viral) types are very catching, so teach hand washing, a separate towel and not sharing eye make-up; allergic conjunctivitis causes itching. Treatment is with the right medicated drops and strict hygiene.

## 2.5 Disorders of the cornea, lens and pressure

**Keratitis** is inflammation or infection of the cornea causing pain, redness, watering and blurred vision; it is serious because scarring reduces sight. Contact-lens misuse is a common cause, so teach correct lens care.

**Cataract** is clouding of the normally clear lens, usually with age but also from diabetes, injury, long steroid use and from birth. Vision becomes gradually blurred, dim and glary, with faded colours. It is treated by surgery — the cloudy lens is removed and an artificial **intraocular lens** is inserted (commonly by phaco-emulsification). After surgery teach the patient not to rub or press the eye, to avoid bending or lifting heavy weights and straining, to wear the protective shield especially at night, to use the prescribed drops correctly, and to report sudden pain, redness or loss of vision.

**Glaucoma** is a group of diseases in which raised eye pressure (or poor blood flow) damages the optic nerve and slowly destroys the field of vision, starting at the sides. *Open-angle glaucoma* is slow and silent — often no symptoms until sight is already lost, so screening matters. *Acute angle-closure glaucoma* is a sudden emergency with severe eye pain, headache, blurred vision with coloured haloes around lights, a red eye and vomiting. Management lowers the pressure with drops and medicines, laser or surgery (trabeculectomy). Lost vision cannot be regained, so **early detection and lifelong treatment** are the key message.

## 2.6 Retina, blindness and other emergencies

**Retinal detachment** is separation of the retina from its blood supply; the patient reports sudden floaters, flashes of light and a curtain or shadow across the vision. It is an emergency needing urgent surgery (laser, buckling or vitrectomy); rest the patient with the head positioned as ordered and avoid sudden movement.

**Blindness** may be avoidable (cataract, refractive error, glaucoma, infection, vitamin A deficiency, diabetic retinopathy) or unavoidable. Prevention through the national eye-care programme, cataract surgery, vitamin A for children, control of diabetes and blood pressure, and eye-injury safety is central. For a person with low vision or blindness the nurse arranges orientation, mobility aids, large print or Braille, a guide, and keeps the surroundings safe and consistent.

**Chemical eye injury** is a first-aid emergency: flush the eye at once with plenty of clean water or saline for a long time before anything else — *delay increases damage.*

## 2.7 Eye donation, banking and transplantation

**Corneal transplantation (keratoplasty)** replaces a scarred or diseased cornea with a healthy donor cornea, restoring sight. The cornea comes from an **eye bank**, which collects, tests and stores donated eyes.

- **Eye donation** is the gift of eyes after death. Any person can pledge; the family's consent is needed at the time. The eyes are removed within a few hours of death by trained staff, so the family should keep the body cool, close the eyes, raise the head slightly and contact the eye bank quickly.
- **Who can donate:** most people regardless of age or spectacle use. The cornea is not used if the donor had certain infections (such as HIV, hepatitis, rabies) or some other conditions; the eye bank screens for these.
- **Nurse's role:** motivate and give correct information to remove fear and myths, counsel grieving families sensitively, help with consent and paperwork, provide the simple after-death care above, and support eye-donation awareness drives.

## 2.8 Nursing procedures (with rationale)

**Instilling eye drops/ointment.**
1. Check the order, the eye (right/left) and the expiry; wash hands.
2. Position the patient with the head tilted slightly back.
3. Ask the patient to look up; gently pull down the lower lid to make a small pocket.
4. Drop the medicine into the pocket, not onto the cornea — *the cornea is sensitive and the drop may be blinked out.*
5. Ask the patient to close the eye gently and press on the inner corner for a minute — *this stops the drug draining into the nose and being absorbed.*
6. Wait a few minutes between two different drops; ointment is applied last.

**Eye irrigation.** Explain the procedure, position the head turned toward the affected side with a receiver below the ear, and let fluid run from the inner to the outer corner so it does not wash across the healthy eye.

**Applying an eye bandage/pad.** Close the lid first, place a sterile pad, and tape it firmly but comfortably; teach the patient not to peep under the pad.

## Remember

- Cornea and lens focus light on the retina; aqueous humour keeps up the normal eye pressure.
- Myopia → concave lens; hypermetropia → convex lens; astigmatism → cylindrical lens; presbyopia → reading glasses.
- Cataract = cloudy lens, treated by removal plus an intraocular lens; after surgery no rubbing, bending or straining, use the shield.
- Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and the side field; open-angle is silent, angle-closure is a painful emergency; lost sight cannot return, so screen and treat early.
- Retinal detachment = floaters, flashes and a curtain over vision — urgent surgery.
- Chemical eye burn: flush immediately with lots of water before anything else.
- Eye drops go into the lower-lid pocket; press the inner corner afterwards to limit systemic absorption.
- Eye donation is after death, within a few hours; the family keeps the eyes closed, head raised, body cool, and calls the eye bank; the nurse counsels and removes myths.

# Unit 3: Kidney, urinary and male reproductive disorders

This unit covers INC Unit III: anatomy and physiology of the urinary system, assessment, common disorders of the kidney and urinary tract, and selected male reproductive disorders. Learn each condition as cause → pathophysiology → features → investigations → management → nursing care.

---

## 3.1 Review of anatomy and physiology

The two kidneys lie retroperitoneally on the posterior abdominal wall. Each kidney contains about one million **nephrons**, the functional units. Each nephron consists of a glomerulus (a capillary tuft enclosed in Bowman's capsule) and a tubule (proximal convoluted, loop of Henle, distal convoluted, collecting duct).

**Functions of the kidney**

| Function | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Filtration | 180 L of filtrate/day; GFR normally 90–120 mL/min |
| Reabsorption | Most water, glucose, Na+, Cl−, HCO3−, amino acids |
| Secretion | H+, K+, drugs, creatinine (tubular secretion) |
| Excretion | Urea, creatinine, uric acid, drugs, toxins |
| Hormone production | Erythropoietin (stimulates RBC production), renin (blood pressure), active vitamin D (calcium) |
| Acid–base balance | Excretes H+ and retains HCO3− |

Urine passes from the collecting duct → renal pelvis → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra. The bladder stores urine; the internal urethral sphincter is involuntary (smooth muscle) and the external sphincter is voluntary (striated muscle). Micturition (voiding) requires a coordinated reflex: bladder stretch → detrusor contraction → sphincter relaxation.

```text
   Cortex (glomeruli, proximal and distal tubules)
      ↓
   Medulla (loops of Henle, collecting ducts)
      ↓
   Renal pelvis → Ureter → Bladder → Urethra
```

## 3.2 Nursing assessment of the urinary system

**History**: frequency, urgency, dysuria, nocturia, haematuria, loin pain, incontinence, hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling, reduced urine output, swelling, foamy urine, past UTIs, kidney stones, diabetes, hypertension, drug history (nephrotoxic drugs — aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, contrast agents).

**Physical examination**: blood pressure (hypertension is common with renal disease), weight and oedema (pitting around ankles and sacrum), flank/costovertebral angle tenderness (pyelonephritis, calculi), palpate for kidney enlargement (polycystic), bladder distension (retention), external genitalia.

**Urine examination**

| Test | Normal/Abnormal |
| --- | --- |
| Colour | Pale yellow; red (blood), dark amber (concentrated/bilirubin), cloudy (pus/phosphates) |
| Specific gravity | 1.001–1.030; fixed 1.010 in CKD |
| pH | 4.5–8.0; alkaline in infection/vegetarian diet |
| Protein | Negative; ++ to ++++ in nephrotic syndrome, GN, infection |
| Glucose | Negative; positive in diabetes or Fanconi syndrome |
| Ketones | Negative; positive in DKA, starvation |
| Nitrites/leucocytes | Positive = UTI (dipstick screening) |
| RBCs | 0–2/HPF; haematuria in infection, calculi, tumour, GN |
| Casts | Hyaline casts normal; RBC casts = glomerulonephritis; WBC casts = pyelonephritis |

**Blood tests**: urea (normally 7–20 mg/dL), serum creatinine (normally 0.6–1.2 mg/dL), eGFR (estimated GFR — calculated from creatinine, age, sex, race), electrolytes (Na+, K+, Cl−, HCO3−), albumin (low in nephrotic), full blood count (anaemia in CKD), uric acid.

**Imaging**: ultrasound (first-line, size/obstruction/stones), plain X-ray KUB (radiopaque calculi), intravenous urography (IVU/IVP), CT urogram (calculi/tumour), cystoscopy (direct bladder/urethra view), renal biopsy (definitive for GN).

## 3.3 Urinary tract infections (UTI)

**Urinary tract infections** are caused by ascending bacteria, most commonly *Escherichia coli* (80%), also *Klebsiella*, *Proteus*, *Staphylococcus saprophyticus*. They are more common in women (short urethra, proximity to anus) and in patients with catheters.

### Lower UTI: cystitis

- Features: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, cloudy or malodorous urine; no fever unless upper tract is involved.
- Investigations: urine dipstick, urine culture and sensitivity (MSU/mid-stream urine).
- Treatment: oral antibiotics — nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim, or cotrimoxazole for 3–7 days; increase fluid intake.
- Nursing: encourage fluid intake (2–3 L/day), complete the antibiotic course, perineal hygiene (wipe front to back), void after intercourse, avoid prolonged catheterisation.

### Upper UTI: pyelonephritis

- Features: high fever with rigors, loin pain and tenderness, nausea, vomiting, plus lower urinary symptoms.
- May be associated with urinary obstruction (calculus, BPH) or vesicoureteric reflux.
- Treatment: IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone, gentamicin) if systemically unwell, then oral; treat the underlying obstruction if present.
- Nursing: temperature monitoring, adequate hydration (IV then oral), analgesia, antipyretics, blood and urine cultures before antibiotics.

### Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI)

CAUTI is the most common hospital-acquired infection. Prevention is paramount:
- Insert catheters only when essential (surgical, retention, accurate output monitoring in critically ill).
- Use aseptic technique during insertion.
- Maintain a closed drainage system; keep the bag below the level of the bladder.
- Secure the catheter to the thigh to prevent movement.
- Perform catheter care with soap and water twice daily.
- Review the need daily and remove as soon as possible.
- Do not routinely change catheters or take cultures without clinical indication.

## 3.4 Urinary incontinence

**Urinary incontinence** (UI) is involuntary loss of urine. It is common in older adults and women but should not be accepted as normal.

| Type | Mechanism | Features | Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stress | Weak pelvic floor/sphincter | Leaks with cough, sneeze, exercise | Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, bladder training, surgery (TVT) |
| Urge | Detrusor overactivity (OAB) | Sudden urge, cannot reach toilet in time | Bladder training, antimuscarinics (oxybutynin, tolterodine) |
| Overflow | Incomplete emptying | Dribbling, distended bladder | Treat obstruction, catheterisation, alpha-blockers (BPH) |
| Functional | Cognitive/physical disability | Cannot reach toilet | Toileting schedule, assistive devices, environmental changes |
| Mixed | Combination of stress + urge | Mixed symptoms | Combined management |

**Nursing management of incontinence**
- Bladder diary (frequency, volume, leaks, triggers) for 3 days.
- Bladder training: gradually increase intervals between voiding.
- Prompted/scheduled voiding for cognitively impaired.
- Perineal skin care: keep dry, barrier cream to prevent dermatitis/pressure sores.
- Pelvic floor exercises: contract, hold 5–10 seconds, release, 10–15 repetitions 3×/day.
- Avoid bladder irritants: caffeine, fizzy drinks, excessive fluid at night.
- Pads/incontinence products as a last resort (not a first choice).

## 3.5 Urinary retention

**Urinary retention** is inability to void despite a full bladder. Acute retention is painful and requires urgent catheterisation. Chronic retention is painless overflow.

**Causes**: BPH (most common in older men), urethral stricture, drugs (anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, opioids), spinal cord injury, post-operative (spinal anaesthesia, perineal surgery), prostate cancer.

**Management**:
- Urethral catheterisation (usually 14–16 Fr Foley catheter) under aseptic technique; drain bladder slowly in acute retention to avoid haematuria from decompression.
- Suprapubic catheter if urethral route is not possible.
- Treat the underlying cause (alpha-blockers for BPH — tamsulosin; surgery for obstruction).
- Monitor urine output after catheter removal (trial without catheter, TWOC).

## 3.6 Renal calculi (kidney stones)

**Renal calculi** are stones in the urinary tract formed from crystallised minerals.

| Type | Composition | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcium oxalate | Most common (~75%) | Radiopaque on X-ray, hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria |
| Uric acid | ~10% | Radiolucent, seen in gout, dehydration |
| Struvite (triple phosphate) | ~15% | Staghorn calculi, associated with urease-producing bacteria (*Proteus*) |
| Cystine | Rare | Hereditary cystinuria |

**Features**: sudden-onset, severe, colicky loin-to-groin pain (ureteric colic), nausea, vomiting, haematuria (frank or microscopic), restlessness; the patient cannot find a comfortable position.

**Investigations**: urine dipstick (blood), ultrasound (obstruction/hydronephrosis), CT urogram (most sensitive — detects all types), stone analysis after passage.

**Management**:
- Analgesia: diclofenac (NSAID) or IV pethidine/morphine; parenteral route until pain controlled.
- IV or oral hydration (2–3 L/day) to flush stone.
- Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) aid stone expulsion.
- Stones <5 mm usually pass spontaneously; >10 mm often need intervention.
- Intervention: extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) for large stones.

**Nursing care**:
- Adequate analgesia and anti-emetics; reassure patient.
- Strain all urine (use a filter or gauge) to catch passed stones for analysis.
- Encourage fluids unless contraindicated.
- Dietary advice: reduce oxalate-rich foods (spinach, tea, nuts) for calcium oxalate stones; reduce red meat and purine-rich foods for uric acid stones; reduce dietary salt and animal protein.
- Teach warning signs of infection (fever, rigors) → immediate medical attention.

## 3.7 Glomerulonephritis and nephritic syndrome

**Glomerulonephritis (GN)** is inflammation of the glomeruli. **Nephritic syndrome** is the clinical presentation of an acute aggressive GN: haematuria, oliguria, hypertension, mild proteinuria, oedema.

**Post-streptococcal GN (PSGN)** is the classic example — occurs 1–4 weeks after throat or skin infection with group A beta-haemolytic *Streptococcus*. It is more common in children.

| Feature | Nephritic syndrome | Nephrotic syndrome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main problem | Inflammation of glomerulus | Increased permeability to protein |
| Proteinuria | Mild (< 3.5 g/day) | Massive (> 3.5 g/day) |
| Haematuria | Prominent, RBC casts | Absent or mild |
| Oedema | Mild periorbital | Severe (generalised anasarca) |
| Hypertension | Present | Variable |
| Plasma albumin | Near normal | Very low |
| Main cause | PSGN, IgA nephropathy, lupus | Minimal change disease (children), membranous nephropathy (adults), diabetes, amyloid |

**Management of PSGN**:
- Rest; fluid restriction matching output + insensible losses.
- Sodium restriction (low-salt diet) for hypertension and oedema.
- Antihypertensives (nifedipine, hydralazine acutely; ACE inhibitors long-term).
- Penicillin to eradicate streptococcal infection.
- Monitor blood pressure, urine output, weight, electrolytes.
- Most patients recover fully; dialysis if severe uraemia or oliguria persists.

## 3.8 Nephrotic syndrome

**Nephrotic syndrome** = proteinuria > 3.5 g/day + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema + hyperlipidaemia + lipiduria.

- In children, **minimal change disease** is the commonest cause; responds well to corticosteroids.
- In adults, **membranous nephropathy**, **focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)**, diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis.

**Management**:
- Corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for minimal change disease).
- Diuretics for oedema (furosemide, spironolactone) — cautiously to avoid volume depletion.
- ACE inhibitors reduce proteinuria.
- Statins for hyperlipidaemia.
- Low-sodium diet; protein intake should be adequate (not excessively restricted).
- Prophylactic anticoagulation considered (risk of deep vein thrombosis and renal vein thrombosis).

**Nursing care**: daily weight, fluid balance, blood pressure 4-hourly, urine protein (dipstick daily), skin care for severe oedema (position changes, avoid pressure), infection prevention (immunocompromised on steroids — isolation, oral care, hand hygiene), steroid education (take with food, do not stop suddenly, weight gain, mood changes).

## 3.9 Acute kidney injury (AKI)

**AKI** (formerly acute renal failure) is a sudden decrease in kidney function over hours to days, causing accumulation of nitrogenous waste and fluid/electrolyte disturbances.

| Classification | Cause | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prerenal | Reduced renal perfusion | Hypovolaemia (haemorrhage, burns, diarrhoea), heart failure, septic shock, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors |
| Intrarenal (Intrinsic) | Direct kidney damage | Acute tubular necrosis (ATN — ischaemia, nephrotoxins), GN, vasculitis |
| Postrenal | Obstruction to outflow | Calculi, BPH, tumour, bilateral ureteric obstruction |

**Features**: oliguria or anuria (< 400 mL/day or < 0.5 mL/kg/h), rising creatinine and urea, hyperkalaemia (most dangerous — arrhythmias), metabolic acidosis, fluid overload (oedema, hypertension), uraemic symptoms (nausea, confusion, pericarditis in severe).

**Management**:
- Treat the cause: fluids for prerenal; relieve obstruction for postrenal.
- Fluid challenge (500 mL 0.9% NaCl over 30–60 min) if hypovolaemic.
- Hyperkalaemia: ECG monitoring; IV calcium gluconate (cardioprotective), insulin-dextrose (shifts K+ intracellularly), salbutamol nebuliser, consider dialysis if >6.5 mEq/L or ECG changes.
- Restrict potassium and phosphate in diet.
- Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, contrast agents) or dose-adjust for GFR.
- Renal replacement therapy (haemodialysis, haemofiltration) indications: refractory hyperkalaemia, volume overload, severe acidosis, uraemic symptoms.

**Nursing care**:
- Strict hourly urine output (catheterise if not voiding).
- Daily weight; fluid balance chart.
- Restrict fluid intake to previous hour's output + 500 mL/day (insensible) if oliguric.
- Cardiac monitoring for hyperkalaemia.
- Avoid nephrotoxic drugs, contrast, and NSAIDs.
- Nutrition: low potassium and phosphate, adequate calories (glucose and fat), limit protein in severe uraemia.

## 3.10 Chronic kidney disease (CKD)

**CKD** is a progressive, irreversible loss of kidney function over > 3 months.

| Stage | GFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | ≥ 90 | Normal or increased GFR, kidney damage markers present |
| 2 | 60–89 | Mildly decreased |
| 3a / 3b | 45–59 / 30–44 | Moderately decreased |
| 4 | 15–29 | Severely decreased |
| 5 | < 15 | Kidney failure (uraemia, need replacement therapy) |

**Common causes**: diabetes mellitus (commonest worldwide — diabetic nephropathy), hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease, obstructive uropathy.

**Complications**: hypertension, anaemia (low erythropoietin — treat with erythropoietin-stimulating agents + iron), renal osteodystrophy (low active vitamin D → secondary hyperparathyroidism → bone disease), fluid/electrolyte disturbances (hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia), cardiovascular disease (leading cause of death in CKD), uraemic symptoms (nausea, pruritus, fatigue, restless legs, peripheral neuropathy, pericarditis).

**Renal replacement therapy (RRT)**:

| Type | Principle | Access | Nursing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Haemodialysis (HD) | Blood passes through extracorporeal dialyser; toxins and fluid removed by diffusion/ultrafiltration | Arteriovenous fistula (preferred), graft, or tunnelled line | Feel the fistula thrill and brachial pulse; never BP, blood draw or IV in the fistula arm; cannulate the fistula with aseptic technique |
| Peritoneal dialysis (PD) | Dialysate infused into peritoneal cavity; peritoneum acts as membrane | Tenckhoff catheter (permanent) | Sterile technique for bag exchanges; watch for peritonitis (cloudy effluent, abdominal pain, fever) → send effluent for C&S |
| Kidney transplant | Best long-term option | Donor kidney placed in iliac fossa | Immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisolone) — lifelong; watch for rejection, infection (immunocompromised) |

**Renal diet in CKD**: restrict potassium (avoid bananas, oranges, tomatoes, potatoes, nuts), phosphate (reduce dairy, meat, colas), sodium (no added salt, avoid processed foods), fluid (500 mL + previous day's urine output), and ensure adequate calorie intake to prevent malnutrition.

**Nursing care in CKD/HD**: monitor interdialytic weight gain (< 2 kg between sessions), blood pressure, fistula care (no constriction — no BP, no blood draw, no IV drip in that arm), dialysis access care, skin care for pruritus (moisturisers, antihistamines), encourage adherence to medications and diet, address psychological impact of chronic illness.

## 3.11 Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

**BPH** is a non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland common in men over 50. The enlarged prostate compresses the urethra, causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS).

**Features**: urinary frequency, nocturia, urgency, hesitancy (waiting for the stream to start), weak/interrupted stream, feeling of incomplete emptying, post-void dribbling, eventually urinary retention or overflow incontinence.

**Investigations**: digital rectal examination (smooth, rubbery, enlarged prostate), urine flow rate and residual volume ultrasound, PSA (to exclude cancer — usually < 10 ng/mL in BPH, often > 10 in cancer), cystoscopy.

**Management**:
- Watchful waiting for mild symptoms.
- Medical: alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin) relax smooth muscle quickly; 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride) shrink the prostate over months — often used together.
- Surgical: TURP (transurethral resection of the prostate) — most common; laser prostatectomy.

**Nursing care post-TURP**:
- Three-way catheter with continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) using 0.9% NaCl to clear haematuria.
- Monitor output of irrigation fluid — input must equal or exceed output (stop if output less than input, may indicate clot obstruction → irrigate manually as ordered).
- Colour of urine: initially red → pink → clear (usually 24–48 h).
- Pain management; encourage leg exercises (DVT risk).
- Remove catheter when urine is clear (usually day 2–3); monitor first void after removal.
- Teach: some bleeding and clots may pass for 2–3 weeks post discharge; avoid constipation, heavy lifting and sexual intercourse for 4–6 weeks.
- Complication: retrograde ejaculation (semen goes into bladder not externally) — reassure, it is not dangerous but affects fertility.

## 3.12 Prostate cancer

**Prostate cancer** is the most common cancer in elderly men. Most are slow-growing adenocarcinomas arising in the peripheral zone. It tends to metastasise to bone (osteoblastic metastases).

**Features**: often asymptomatic early; LUTS, haematuria, bone pain (back, pelvis, hips), weight loss in advanced disease.

**Investigations**: PSA (elevated — usually > 10 ng/mL, may be higher in cancer but also raised in BPH and prostatitis; trending matters more than a single value), digital rectal examination (hard, irregular, asymmetric prostate), transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy (definitive), bone scan (for metastases), MRI prostate (staging).

**Management**:
- Active surveillance: for low-risk, well-differentiated disease; PSA and biopsy repeated.
- Radical prostatectomy (open or robotic-assisted laparoscopic).
- Radiotherapy (external beam, or brachytherapy — seeds implanted).
- Hormone therapy (androgen deprivation) — LHRH agonists (goserelin, leuprolide) or orchidectomy — for metastatic disease.
- Chemotherapy (docetaxel) for castration-resistant prostate cancer.

**Nursing care**: pre- and post-operative care for prostatectomy (including catheter care and pelvic floor exercises for continence recovery), manage complications of hormone therapy (hot flushes, osteoporosis, fatigue, mood changes), bone pain management, psychological support, PSA follow-up education.

# Unit 4: Burns, reconstructive and cosmetic surgery

This unit covers INC Unit IV: classification, assessment and management of burns, principles of reconstructive surgery, and an overview of cosmetic procedures. Burns nursing is a high-acuity specialty; mastering fluid resuscitation, wound care and infection prevention saves lives.

---

## 4.1 Classification of burns

Burns are injuries to the skin and underlying tissues caused by heat, chemicals, electricity, radiation or friction.

### By depth

| Degree | Former name | Depth | Appearance | Sensation | Healing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Superficial (1st degree) | First degree | Epidermis only | Red, dry, no blisters | Painful | 3–5 days, no scar |
| Superficial partial-thickness | Second degree | Epidermis + superficial dermis | Red, wet, blisters | Very painful | 7–14 days, minimal scar |
| Deep partial-thickness | Deep second degree | Epidermis + deep dermis | White/mottled, dry, blisters may be absent | Decreased (dermis damaged) | 14–35 days, scar likely; may need grafting |
| Full-thickness (3rd degree) | Third degree | Full skin thickness | White, brown or black, leathery, dry | Painless (nerve endings destroyed) | Cannot self-heal; requires grafting |
| Fourth degree | — | Skin + underlying fat, muscle, bone | Charred, black | Painless | Requires debridement ± amputation |

### By cause

- **Thermal**: flame, hot liquids (scalds), steam, hot solids (contact burns).
- **Chemical**: acids, alkalis, phosphorus. Alkali burns are deeper (liquefactive necrosis) and more serious than acid burns.
- **Electrical**: entry and exit wounds; internal damage along current path (muscle necrosis, arrhythmia, renal failure from myoglobinuria). Current follows nerves and blood vessels, so visible skin injury underestimates the total.
- **Radiation**: sunburn (ultraviolet), X-ray or nuclear exposure.

## 4.2 Assessment of burn size

### Rule of Nines (adults)

```text
           Head and neck      9%
   Right arm      9%   Left arm      9%
   Anterior trunk  18%
   Posterior trunk 18%
   Right leg      18%   Left leg      18%
   Perineum        1%
                        TOTAL = 100%
```

### Lund and Browder chart

More accurate than the rule of nines; adjusts for age because children have proportionally larger heads and smaller legs. Used for children and large burns.

### Palmar surface method

The patient's palm (including fingers) ≈ 1% TBSA; useful for scattered burns.

**Note**: Superficial (first-degree) burns such as ordinary sunburn are **not included** in the TBSA calculation used for fluid resuscitation.

### Inhalation injury — recognition is critical

Suspect inhalation injury when:
- Burn occurred in an enclosed space.
- Singed nasal hairs or eyebrows.
- Soot in nostrils, mouth, or sputum.
- Hoarse voice, stridor (upper airway oedema — can close within hours).
- Burns to face, neck, or oral cavity.

**Action**: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask at once; early intubation before the airway swells shut; call anaesthetics/ICU urgently.

## 4.3 Burn shock and fluid resuscitation

### Pathophysiology of burn shock

Large burns cause massive release of inflammatory mediators (histamine, prostaglandins, cytokines) → vasodilation and dramatically increased capillary permeability. Plasma leaks from capillaries into the interstitium ("third-spacing"), causing:
- Hypovolaemia and reduced cardiac output (shock).
- Local oedema at the wound and distant oedema.
- Haemoconcentration (rising haematocrit as plasma is lost).

```text
   Burn injury
      ↓
   Inflammatory mediators released
      ↓
   Capillary leak (massive fluid shift to interstitium)
      ↓
   Hypovolaemia + oedema
      ↓
   Decreased organ perfusion (kidneys, gut, heart)
      ↓
   Multi-organ failure if not corrected
```

This capillary leak is greatest in the first 24 hours and largely stops by 48 hours.

### Parkland formula for fluid resuscitation

**4 mL × body weight (kg) × % TBSA burned = total fluid in first 24 hours**

Use Hartmann's solution (Ringer's lactate) in the first 24 hours.

- Give **half** in the **first 8 hours** from the **time of injury** (not from arrival).
- Give the remaining **half** in the **next 16 hours**.

**Example**: 70 kg adult with 30% TBSA burns.
4 × 70 × 30 = 8,400 mL total.
Give 4,200 mL in 8 hours, then 4,200 mL in 16 hours.

**Target urine output**: 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (30–50 mL/h), 1 mL/kg/h in children — this is the best guide to adequate resuscitation. Adjust fluid rate according to urine output.

After 24 hours, colloids (albumin, FFP) may be added, and oral intake starts as tolerated.

## 4.4 Burn wound care

### First aid

- **Stop the burning**: remove from source, remove clothing (not stuck clothing), remove jewellery and watches before oedema makes this impossible.
- **Cool the burn**: cool running water (15–20°C) for 20 minutes — started within 3 hours of burn; do not use ice (causes frostbite and worsens injury).
- **Cover**: with a clean (ideally sterile) low-adherence dressing or cling film; do not burst blisters.

### Wound management

**Wound debridement**: removal of dead tissue (eschar), either:
- **Conservative**: daily cleansing and dressings; eschar separates gradually.
- **Surgical**: tangential excision under general anaesthesia — faster, reduces infection risk.

**Dressings**:
- Silver sulfadiazine (Flamazine) 1% cream — broad antibacterial cover; apply daily; can cause leucopenia with extended use.
- Silver-containing dressings (Mepitel Ag, Aquacel Ag) — fewer dressing changes (every 2–7 days), reduce pain.
- Biological dressings (allograft from cadaver, xenograft from pig, amniotic membrane) — temporary coverage until autograft is available.
- Synthetic substitutes (Biobrane, Integra) — for large burns without enough donor skin.

**Skin grafting**:
- **Split-thickness skin graft (STSG)**: the most common; epidermis + part of dermis harvested from a donor site (thigh, back, buttock) using a dermatome; can be meshed to cover a larger area; donor site heals in 10–14 days with epithelial cells from hair follicles.
- **Full-thickness skin graft (FTSG)**: epidermis + full dermis; better cosmetic outcome; donor site must be sutured closed; used for small areas (face, hands).

**Donor site care**: the donor site (where skin was taken) is a painful partial-thickness wound; cover with a simple dressing (paraffin gauze or Mepitel); keep clean and dry; heals in 10–14 days.

## 4.5 Infection prevention

Burns destroy the skin barrier — infection (wound sepsis, pneumonia, septicaemia) is the leading cause of death in burn patients after the first 48 hours.

- **Wound colonisation is inevitable; invasive infection is what must be prevented.**
- Wound cultures twice weekly to track colonising organisms.
- Topical antimicrobials (silver sulfadiazine, mafenide acetate) reduce bacterial load.
- Systemic antibiotics only for clinical infection (fever + wound changes + positive blood/wound cultures) — not prophylactically.
- Strict infection control: handwashing, gloves, aprons; isolated burn unit if available; limit visitors.
- Early wound closure (grafting) is the most effective way to prevent infection.
- Monitor: daily wound inspection for colour change (greenish = *Pseudomonas*, black = *Aspergillus*), odour, cellulitis in surrounding skin, temperature trend.

## 4.6 Nutritional support

Burns dramatically increase metabolic rate (by 1.5–2.5× basal metabolic rate in major burns). Insufficient nutrition → impaired healing, immunosuppression, muscle wasting.

- Nasogastric or nasojejunal tube feeding should start early (within 6 hours of injury) if oral intake is not adequate.
- High-calorie, high-protein diet: aim for 30–35 kcal/kg/day and 1.5–2 g protein/kg/day for major burns.
- Glutamine supplementation reduces infections and hospital stay.
- Monitor weight, prealbumin/albumin, wound healing — these reflect nutritional adequacy.

## 4.7 Pain management

Burns are extremely painful, especially dressing changes.

- Background pain: regular oral/IV analgesia — paracetamol, NSAIDs, oral morphine.
- Procedural (dressing change) pain: IV morphine or ketamine (small dose IV/IM) 20–30 minutes before the procedure; Entonox (nitrous oxide) inhalation during the procedure.
- Psychological support: explain each procedure; allow some patient control over pace of dressing change; music, distraction.
- Itching (pruritus) of healing wounds: antihistamines (chlorpheniramine, cetirizine), moisturisers, cool compresses.

## 4.8 Respiratory care

- Major facial/inhalation burns: endotracheal tube or tracheostomy (early, before oedema closes airway).
- Humidified oxygen to prevent drying of airways.
- Suction every 1–2 hours for secretions (sooty, thick initially).
- Circumferential chest burns → escharotomy (surgical release of eschar) if breathing is restricted.
- Nebulised N-acetylcysteine, heparin and salbutamol to manage chemical airway injury.

## 4.9 Contracture prevention and rehabilitation

Healed burn wounds and grafted skin contract as they mature, forming tight bands (**contractures**) that restrict movement, especially across joints.

- **Positioning**: anti-contracture positions from day one (e.g. neck extended, shoulders abducted, hands in position of safe immobilisation — wrist in slight extension, MCPs flexed, IPs extended, thumb abducted).
- **Splinting**: custom thermoplastic splints made by physiotherapists and occupational therapists; worn at night and when not exercising.
- **Physiotherapy**: range-of-motion exercises twice daily; encourage early ambulation.
- **Pressure garments** (Jobst/Tubigrip): worn 23 hours/day for 12–24 months over healed areas — reduce scar thickness and prevent contracture; must be fitted correctly and replaced when stretched.
- **Surgical release**: Z-plasty, skin grafting, or flap reconstruction for established contractures.

## 4.10 Psychological rehabilitation

Burns cause significant psychological trauma: disfigurement, long hospitalisation, repeated painful procedures, fear, grief, and body image change.

- Encourage the patient to express feelings about their appearance.
- Involve family and significant others from the start.
- Refer to psychologist or psychiatrist early (anxiety, depression, PTSD are common).
- Connect with peer support (burn survivors).
- Realistic counselling about scar progression (scars continue to mature for 12–24 months; laser and reconstructive options are available later).
- Occupational rehabilitation: plan return to work/school; provide vocational guidance if occupation needs to change.

## 4.11 Reconstructive surgery

**Reconstructive surgery** restores form and function after trauma, cancer, burns, or congenital defects. The goal is functional recovery first, then cosmesis.

| Technique | Indication | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary wound closure | Small clean wounds | Suturing edges directly |
| Skin graft (STSG/FTSG) | Burns, ulcers, skin loss | As described above |
| Local flap (Z-plasty, rotation, transposition) | Releasing contracture, closing near the wound | Surrounding tissue rearranged |
| Regional flap | Cover exposed structures | Pedicled flap from nearby area (e.g. gastrocnemius for tibia) |
| Free flap (microvascular) | Major reconstruction | Tissue with its own blood vessels transplanted, anastomosed under microscope |
| Tissue expansion | Scalp, breast, face | Silicone balloon inserted under skin, inflated over weeks; stretched skin used for closure |

**Timing**: acute burns need early excision and grafting; reconstructive procedures for established scars/contractures are done after the wound is stable and mature (6–12 months from injury).

## 4.12 Cosmetic (aesthetic) surgery

**Cosmetic surgery** aims to improve appearance. The nurse's role includes pre-operative counselling, ensuring informed consent, and post-operative care.

**Common procedures and nursing care**:

| Procedure | Purpose | Key nursing points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Liposuction | Remove localised fat deposits | Compression garment 6 weeks; monitor fluid shifts, haematoma, contour irregularity |
| Rhinoplasty (nose job) | Reshape the nose | Ice packs, head elevation (30°), nasal splint, avoid blowing nose, monitor for bleeding |
| Rhytidectomy (face lift) | Reduce facial wrinkles | Drain management, pressure dressings, avoid sun |
| Blepharoplasty | Remove excess eyelid skin | Eye care, cold compresses, follow up for vision changes |
| Breast augmentation | Increase breast size with implants | Drain care, support bra, wound monitoring, teach self-examination |
| Breast reduction | Reduce heavy breasts | Drain care, wound healing, bra support |
| Abdominoplasty (tummy tuck) | Remove excess abdominal skin | Compression garment, DVT prophylaxis, wound care |

**Pre-operative counselling points**: realistic expectations; photographs for comparison; discuss scars (all surgery scars); smoking cessation (impairs healing); stop NSAIDs/aspirin 2 weeks pre-op; psychological readiness; consent covers risks (haematoma, infection, asymmetry, scarring, anaesthesia risks).
